findings.title: Permissive CORS Origin Validation Allows Arbitrary Attacker Origins to Exfiltrate Authenticated User Data
findings.evidence: if (!origin || origin.startsWith(env.clientUrl) || origin.includes('localhost') || origin.includes('pinggy') || origin.includes('trycloudflare')) { return callback(null, true); } return callback(new Error('Not allowed by CORS'));
findings.scenario: An attacker creates a malicious webpage on any domain containing 'localhost' (e.g., https://localhost.attacker.com), 'pinggy' (e.g., https://malicious-pinggy.io), 'trycloudflare' (any Cloudflare quick tunnel), or any subdomain prefixing env.clientUrl (e.g., https://clienturl.com.attacker.com). When a logged-in user visits the attacker's page, malicious JavaScript executes fetch('https://api.domain.com/api/auth/me', { credentials: 'include' }) or '/api/payments/mine'. Because credentials: true is enabled and the origin passes the loose regex/substring check, the browser exposes private user data, tokens, and payment history to the attacker.
findings.impact: Complete cross-origin confidentiality breach. Attacker can read sensitive customer profiles, payment receipts, and issue cross-origin requests using victim's ambient credentials.
findings.reproduction: curl -H "Origin: https://evil-trycloudflare.com" -H "Cookie: refreshToken=fake" http://localhost:5000/api/auth/me -v. Notice Access-Control-Allow-Origin: https://evil-trycloudflare.com and Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true are returned.
findings.remediation: Replace substring matching with an explicit whitelist of fully qualified domain names parsed into an exact Set or Array: const allowedOrigins = new Set([env.clientUrl, 'https://macreation.in']); cors({ origin: (origin, cb) => { if (!origin || allowedOrigins.has(origin)) return cb(null, true); return cb(null, false); }, credentials: true }). Never pass new Error() to CORS callback as it generates 500 internal errors.
findings.regressionTest: Unit test verifying that origins 'https://clienturl.evil.com', 'https://localhost.attacker.com', and 'https://evil.trycloudflare.com' are rejected with Access-Control-Allow-Origin absent and HTTP status clean (no 500 error).

findings.title: Blind Trust Proxy (`app.set('trust proxy', 1)`) Susceptible to Client IP Spoofing and Shared Proxy Lockout
findings.scenario: The application is deployed behind Caddy, Cloudflare, and Docker bridge network. Trusting 1 hop means Express assumes there is only a single trusted reverse proxy. In a multi-hop edge setup (Cloudflare -> Caddy -> Node), the first hop in X-Forwarded-For is an upstream proxy or an internal container IP (e.g. 172.18.0.x). When express-rate-limit and loginRateLimiter look up req.ip, every user sharing that proxy hop gets bundled under the same IP address. One malicious user triggering brute-force lockouts causes all other legitimate users to be rate-limited and locked out (Denial of Service).
findings.impact: Global denial of service for all users behind common edge proxies, or rate-limit evasion by spoofing header values if accessed directly.
findings.reproduction: Send requests with forged X-Forwarded-For: 1.1.1.1, 2.2.2.2. req.ip resolves incorrectly depending on proxy hop count.
findings.remediation: Configure trust proxy to explicitly trust known internal subnet ranges or loopback, e.g., app.set('trust proxy', 'loopback, linklocal, uniquelocal') or configure Caddy to overwrite X-Forwarded-For with the remote client IP directly.
findings.regressionTest: Integration test validating that req.ip accurately extracts client IP when behind Caddy with Docker bridge IPs (172.16.0.0/12).

findings.title: In-Memory Rate Limiting Unshared Across Replicas, Bypassed in Load-Test Mode, and Omits SSE Endpoint
findings.evidence: max: process.env.LOAD_TEST_MODE === 'true' ? 200000 : process.env.NODE_ENV === 'production' ? 1200 : 100000, skip: (req) => process.env.NODE_ENV !== 'production' || process.env.LOAD_TEST_MODE === 'true' || req.path === '/api/public/events' || req.path.startsWith('/api-docs')
findings.scenario: 1) Rate limiting uses the default memory store, which is not synchronized across multi-process or clustered Node instances; 2) If LOAD_TEST_MODE is enabled or NODE_ENV is unset, rate limiting is completely disabled, allowing unlimited automated credential attacks; 3) The Server-Sent Events route (/api/public/events) is explicitly skipped from rate limiting. An attacker can spawn hundreds of concurrent HTTP GET connections to /api/public/events, exhausting server socket descriptors and worker thread capacity.
findings.impact: Exhaustion of HTTP connection pool, memory exhaustion, and inability to throttle distributed brute force across multi-container deployments.
findings.reproduction: Run concurrent curl requests to /api/public/events. The rate limiter skips all of them.
findings.remediation: Use RedisStore (rate-limit-redis) backed by redisConnection for distributed rate tracking across all backend instances. Remove the complete skip bypass for non-production/load-test mode, and apply dedicated connection limiters on /api/public/events.
findings.regressionTest: Verify RedisStore integration and confirm /api/public/events enforces a per-IP connection concurrency cap.

findings.title: Direct Public Host Exposure of MinIO S3 API & Web Console Ports (9000 & 9001)
findings.scenario: docker-compose.yml maps port 9000 (S3 API) and port 9001 (MinIO Web Console) directly to 0.0.0.0 on the host VM. While the documentation and Caddyfile state that Caddy is the only service exposed to the internet, any remote attacker scanning the VPS host IP can connect directly to port 9001 to brute-force the MinIO admin console or to port 9000 to query the S3 API directly, bypassing Caddy SSL, Cloudflare WAF, and all application-level controls.
findings.impact: Direct perimeter breach. Storage management console and S3 API are exposed to the public internet without edge protection or rate limiting.
findings.reproduction: curl http://<SERVER_IP>:9001/minio/health/live. Console web UI responds immediately.
findings.remediation: Remove host port mappings '9000:9000' and '9001:9001' from docker-compose.yml. MinIO should only communicate with backend and worker via the internal docker network (lms_internal), and public presigned URL access should route strictly through Caddy with restricted path proxying.
findings.regressionTest: Port scan verification confirming ports 9000 and 9001 are closed on the public interface.

findings.title: Public Host Exposure of Dozzle Docker Daemon Log Viewer on Port 8080
findings.scenario: Dozzle mounts the host Docker socket (/var/run/docker.sock) and exposes port 8080 to 0.0.0.0 without HTTPS or reverse proxy protection. If DOZZLE_USER and DOZZLE_PASSWORD are weak or unconfigured in production, an attacker connecting to port 8080 gains full real-time access to all container stdout/stderr logs across all services, exposing environment variables, database connection strings, JWT secrets, and customer PII.
findings.impact: Catastrophic sensitive data leakage. Exposure of host container telemetry and application secrets.
findings.reproduction: curl -I http://<SERVER_IP>:8080. Returns Dozzle HTTP login banner.
findings.remediation: Bind Dozzle strictly to loopback (127.0.0.1:8080:8080) for SSH-tunneled administrative access only, or route it through Caddy with strict IP-whitelisting and strong multi-factor authentication.
findings.regressionTest: Check docker-compose port binding to ensure 0.0.0.0:8080 is not listening.

findings.title: Caddy Reverse Proxy Bound Exclusively to Plaintext HTTP Port 80 Without TLS Enforcement
findings.scenario: The Caddyfile specifies :80 instead of a named domain block ({$APP_DOMAIN}). In Caddy, binding explicitly to :80 disables Caddy's Automatic HTTPS engine (Let's Encrypt / ZeroSSL certificate issuance and HTTP-to-HTTPS redirect). All client-to-API communication, including login passwords, bearer tokens, and payment signatures, is transmitted in plaintext over cleartext HTTP.
findings.impact: Eavesdropping, credential sniffing, and man-in-the-middle (MitM) attacks against all web and mobile traffic.
findings.reproduction: Inspect Caddyfile and observe that domain block is commented out and only :80 is active.
findings.remediation: Uncomment and configure {$APP_DOMAIN} block in Caddyfile with automatic HTTPS, HSTS header, and automatic HTTP-to-HTTPS redirection.
findings.regressionTest: Automated curl check verifying that HTTP requests receive 301/308 redirects to HTTPS and HTTPS endpoints serve valid TLS certificates with Strict-Transport-Security headers.

findings.title: Incomplete Graceful Shutdown Leaks Redis Connections and Prematurely Aborts Active Video Transcoding
findings.evidence: async function shutdown(signal) { if (server) { await new Promise(resolve => server.close(resolve)) } await disconnectDB().catch(() => {}) process.exit(0) }
findings.scenario: 1) In server.js, shutdown closes server and disconnects MongoDB, but never closes redisConnection or videoTranscodeQueue, leaving lingering Redis connections and pending queue events; 2) server.close() lacks a timeout fallback, meaning long-lived SSE connections or hung requests will stall the process forever until SIGKILL; 3) In transcode.worker.js, the shutdown handler sets a 2-second timeout (Promise.race([worker.close(), setTimeout(2000)])) before forcing process.exit(0). If a 30-minute video transcode is underway when SIGTERM is sent (e.g. during deployment rollout), FFmpeg is killed after 2 seconds, leaving corrupted video fragments on disk and the MongoDB video record permanently stuck in PROCESSING status.
findings.impact: Interrupted video transcodes, stuck queue jobs, leaked Redis connections, and lingering processes hanging container deployments.
findings.reproduction: Send SIGTERM to transcode.worker while FFmpeg is active. Process exits within 2 seconds without completing job cleanup.
findings.remediation: In server.js, add a 10s shutdown timeout, close redisConnection and videoTranscodeQueue. In transcode.worker.js, permit workers sufficient grace time to pause and release active locks or mark jobs back to QUEUED/FAILED cleanly.
findings.regressionTest: Simulate SIGTERM to server and worker and verify all handles (HTTP, Mongo, Redis, BullMQ) terminate cleanly within bounded window.

findings.title: Default Admin Password Fallback and Shared Video DRM Key Secret in Production Configuration
findings.evidence:
videoDrmSecret: process.env.VIDEO_DRM_SECRET || process.env.JWT_SECRET,
adminEmail: process.env.ADMIN_EMAIL || "admin@macreation.in",
adminPassword: process.env.ADMIN_PASSWORD || "Admin@12345",
findings.scenario: assertProductionEnv() checks MONGODB_URI, JWT_SECRET, and RAZORPAY keys, but completely omits checking ADMIN_PASSWORD and VIDEO_DRM_SECRET. If an operator launches in production without explicitly providing ADMIN_PASSWORD in .env, the application seeds and accepts the publicly known default credentials ('Admin@12345'). Additionally, VIDEO_DRM_SECRET defaults to JWT_SECRET, violating cryptographic separation of concerns.
findings.impact: Immediate administrative takeover if ADMIN_PASSWORD is left unset in production environment.
findings.reproduction: Start application with NODE_ENV=production and omit ADMIN_PASSWORD. Server starts successfully and accepts default Admin@12345 password.
findings.remediation: Include ADMIN_PASSWORD and VIDEO_DRM_SECRET in assertProductionEnv() required fields. Prevent fallback to default passwords when NODE_ENV is production.
findings.regressionTest: Unit test asserting that assertProductionEnv() throws when ADMIN_PASSWORD or VIDEO_DRM_SECRET is unset in production.

findings.title: High-Concurrency Compound MongoDB Indexes Commented Out in Mongoose Schema Models
findings.scenario: Critical performance compound indexes that optimize entitlement checks (Payment.find({ user, plan, status: 'paid' })), video listings, playback session validations, and token revocation checks were created manually in an ad-hoc script (ensure-indexes.js) but commented out in the actual Mongoose models. In new deployments, automated tests, or database failovers where ensure-indexes.js is not executed manually, MongoDB falls back to COLLSCAN (full collection scans) on every video stream, entitlement check, and login refresh, causing high CPU spikes and database denial of service under concurrency.
findings.impact: Database bottleneck and high query latency (COLLSCAN) causing cascade request timeouts under normal student load.
findings.reproduction: Inspect models/LMS/Payment.js, models/LMS/Video.js, models/LMS/PlaybackSession.js, models/AUTH/RefreshToken.js. Observe compound indexes are commented out.
findings.remediation: Uncomment compound indexes in all Mongoose schema definitions so they are indexed automatically during collection initialization.
findings.regressionTest: Execute diagnose-db-scans script against fresh database and confirm 0 unindexed queries on Payment, Video, PlaybackSession, and RefreshToken collections.

findings.title: Content Security Policy (CSP) Globally Disabled in Helmet Configuration
findings.scenario: Helmet's contentSecurityPolicy is disabled globally across the Express application to accommodate Swagger UI. Because CSP is disabled for all routes, any HTML served by the application (including Swagger UI fallback, error responses, or future endpoints) lacks Content-Security-Policy protection against cross-site scripting (XSS), script injection, or malicious iframe embedding.
findings.impact: Absence of defense-in-depth against client-side script injection and iframe manipulation.
findings.reproduction: curl -I http://localhost:5000/api/health. Observe absence of Content-Security-Policy header in response.
findings.remediation: Enable a strict default CSP for the general API (contentSecurityPolicy: { directives: { defaultSrc: ["'none'"] } }), and apply a customized relaxed CSP specifically to the /api-docs route only.
findings.regressionTest: Check response headers for /api/health to confirm Content-Security-Policy header is present with secure defaults.

findings.title: Refresh CSRF Guard Contracts Mismatch Between Mobile App Documentation and Enforcement Logic
findings.scenario: In backend/src/config/swagger.js, mobile clients (Flutter developers) are instructed to send 'x-client-platform: APP'. However, refreshCsrfGuard strictly checks for 'MOBILE_IOS' or 'MOBILE_ANDROID'. When a Flutter mobile client sends 'APP', the check evaluates to false and falls through to the web requirement ('x-refresh-token: 1'), rejecting valid mobile token refreshes with 403 FORBIDDEN. Conversely, any web browser hitting this endpoint can bypass the CSRF guard if CORS allows arbitrary origins and the request includes 'x-client-platform: MOBILE_ANDROID'.
findings.impact: Legitimate Flutter mobile applications fail token renewal in production, or web clients can bypass CSRF checks if custom headers are exposed.
findings.reproduction: Send POST /api/auth/refresh with header x-client-platform: APP. Response is 403 Forbidden: CSRF check failed.
findings.remediation: Align the platform check to accept 'APP' and ensure mobile requests carry bearer/body authentication rather than ambient cookies, validating that the platform header matches the token platform type stored in the database.
findings.regressionTest: Verify /api/auth/refresh responds with 200 when presented with valid refresh token and header 'x-client-platform: APP'.

findings.title: Unhandled Promise Rejections Logged Without Initiating Clean Process Shutdown
findings.scenario: When an unhandled asynchronous error occurs, the server logs to console and continues execution. Unhandled promise rejections often leave MongoDB connection pools, BullMQ queue events, or HTTP file streams in undefined or half-open states, causing silent cascading failures until manual restart.
findings.impact: Silent corruption of asynchronous workflows and hanging database transactions.
findings.reproduction: Trigger an asynchronous unhandled rejection. Server logs the error but remains running with corrupted state.
findings.remediation: Log the unhandled rejection to Sentry/logger and initiate shutdown('unhandledRejection') so the process manager (Docker/systemd) can launch a healthy replacement container.
findings.regressionTest: Verify unhandledRejection logs critical alert and triggers graceful shutdown procedure with non-zero exit code.

findings.title: Global Error Handler Leaks Stack Traces in Non-Production and Internal Database Keys
findings.evidence:
const field = Object.keys(err.keyValue || {})[0]
message = `Duplicate value: '${field}' already exists in database`
...
...(isProd ? {} : (status >= 500 && err.stack ? { stack: err.stack } : {}))
findings.scenario: If NODE_ENV is not explicitly set to 'production' (e.g. staging or QA environments), full stack traces including internal server file paths and line numbers are exposed in API JSON responses. Furthermore, duplicate key errors explicitly disclose internal MongoDB collection field names to unauthenticated users.
findings.impact: Information disclosure of internal server architecture and schema structures.
findings.reproduction: Trigger a 500 or duplicate key error in staging/local mode. Response includes stack trace and err.keyValue.
findings.remediation: Enforce strict generic messages for 500 errors and sanitize database error messages to avoid revealing schema field names.
findings.regressionTest: Verify errorHandler returns standardized error envelopes without stack or schema internals regardless of NODE_ENV.

findings.title: MinIO Video Bucket Initialization Does Not Enforce Explicit Private Read Policy
findings.scenario: ensureVideoBucket checks if the bucket exists, but does not verify or assert its bucket policy. If the bucket was pre-created with an anonymous read policy or modified out-of-band, video chunks and course materials could be accessed directly without presigned URLs.
findings.impact: Potential direct unauthorized download of premium course videos bypassing watch limits and billing entitlements.
findings.reproduction: Create bucket with public policy; run ensureVideoBucket(); bucket policy remains public.
findings.remediation: Call minioClient.setBucketPolicy(BUCKET, '') or verify getBucketPolicy returns no anonymous access policy during server boot.
findings.regressionTest: Verify startup hook validates and enforces private access policy on MinIO video bucket.

findings.title: Razorpay Payment Webhook Lacks Explicit Raw Body Size Limit
findings.scenario: express.raw({ type: 'application/json' }) is registered without an explicit limit option (defaulting to Express's 100kb limit). If the global body parser or Express configuration is updated, unbounded raw request body buffering can lead to memory exhaustion on webhook endpoints.
findings.impact: Resource allocation vulnerability on public webhook endpoint.
findings.reproduction: Send large payload to /api/payments/webhook without explicit limit guard.
findings.remediation: Specify explicit defensive limit: express.raw({ type: 'application/json', limit: '100kb' }).
findings.regressionTest: Verify payload exceeding 100kb is rejected with 413 Payload Too Large on webhook endpoint.

notes: Comprehensive architecture and edge perimeter audit executed following edge-perimeter-guard and QA canonical contract.
No application source code or existing tests were modified during this audit.
